events.note: The dated watch list behind the Events view: hearings, rulings, deadlines, and elections, grouped in chronological phases. Dates are labels as published; judge nearness against as_of.

events.title: Pied-a-terre owner notices due; first compliance deadline of the new tax.
events.detail: New York enacted an annual surcharge on NYC residences that are not the owner’s primary home, effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2031, projected at roughly $500 million per year from about 10,000 to 13,000 properties. Condos and co-ops assessed at $1 million or more pay 4%, 5.25%, or 6.5% by tier; one-to-three-family homes at $5 million or more pay 0.8% to 1.3%. Owners must file notices establishing primary-residence status by Aug. 30; the Department of Finance finalized its implementation rules on July 14, 2026, covering residency determinations and audits, and exemption application deadlines were extended to Sept. 18. Why it matters: this is the first big-city tax keyed to property ownership rather than income, a template other cities are watching, and its rollout will show whether valuation and residency disputes make wealth-adjacent taxes administrable. Legal exposure is now live: on Aug. 7, 2026, three homeowners represented by former Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro sued in Richmond County Supreme Court over the rollout, and on Aug. 10 Justice Wayne M. Ozzi issued a temporary restraining order halting the published supplemental roll of about 900,000 properties, further notices to roughly 17,000 homeowners, and collection steps; the city’s appeal stays the order, and a hearing is set for Aug. 31, one day after the notice deadline.

events.title: Democratic gubernatorial primary.
events.detail: Rhode Island enacted a phased millionaires surtax in June (1% on income over $1M in 2027, rising to 3% by 2029, top rate to 8.99%) plus a 0.5% annual surcharge on non-owner-occupied homes assessed over $1M. The primary decides whether the party’s nominee comes from the wing that treated the enacted surtax as the compromise or the wing backing the broader Fair Share package (H 7313 / S 2238: a 3% surtax starting at $640K plus a 1% annual tax on financial assets over $25M, which would be the first true state wealth tax in America). Why it matters: the winner shapes whether Rhode Island’s 2027 session stops at the enacted phase-in or reopens the wealth tax question.

events.title: Secretary’s voter information booklet publishes for all nine certified questions.
events.detail: Nine statewide questions were certified in July for the Nov. 3 ballot, tying the modern record set in 1972, 1976, and 1994, including the Chapter 62F rewrite (Question 5). The September booklet mails the official summaries and for/against arguments to every household, the single largest voter touchpoint before election day. Why it matters: 62F polling is soft and low-information; the official framing that lands in every mailbox materially shapes the outcome.

events.title: Petter v. Dept. of Revenue trial ruling, Klickitat County Superior Court.
events.detail: The issue: whether Washington’s new 9.9% tax on income over $1M (SB 6346, effective 2028) violates the state constitution. Under Culliton v. Chase (1933), income is property in Washington, and the constitution requires property to be taxed uniformly and caps it at 1%, which is why the state has never had a graduated income tax. Plaintiffs (business owners and trade associations, represented by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former Justice Phil Talmadge) seek a declaratory judgment voiding the tax; the state will argue it is an excise, the theory that saved the capital gains tax in 2023. Potential impact: if struck down, the Department of Revenue's revised projection of $3.1 billion in the first fiscal year from an estimated 25,000 households (up from $2.7 billion and 21,000 filers in the original fiscal note) disappears and the 90-year wall against graduated income taxation holds, chilling copycats in Oregon and beyond. If upheld, the wall falls in the state that built it. No ruling reported as of August 14, 2026; final resolution expected at the state Supreme Court in early 2027.

events.title: Proposition 40 and Proposition 3 both resolve.
events.detail: Prop 40 is a one-time 5% tax on net worth above $1 billion, covering resident individuals and applicable trusts, structured as a combined constitutional amendment and statute, the only true wealth tax on any American ballot, qualified with 980,438 valid signatures. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts are excluded; payment is due in 2027 or in five-year installments. Building a Better California, the opposition committee co-founded by Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt, has reported more than $118 million raised, including $102 million contributed personally by Brin per filings disclosed through Aug. 7, 2026; supporters report $31.4 million (SF Examiner, Secretary of State disclosures). Collectively the committees for and against Propositions 40, 41, and 42 have raised $140 million. The California Democratic Party endorsed the measure in a narrow executive-board vote in early August. Prop 3, sharing the ballot, would make the Prop 30-era top income brackets (top combined rate 13.3%) permanent past their scheduled expiration after tax year 2030. Potential impact: a Prop 40 win is the first voter-approved wealth tax in US history and the national template; a loss after $80M+ against it becomes the cautionary tale every other state coalition must answer. Either way, the result recalibrates every state’s risk overnight.

events.title: Initiative 645: repeal of the millionaires tax.
events.detail: Certified for the ballot on July 15, 2026 with more than 500,000 signatures against a 308,911 requirement, I-645 (Let’s Go Washington) would repeal SB 6346 and prohibit state and local taxes on individual income. Why it matters: this is the direct democratic verdict on the tax, running in parallel with the Petter litigation; repeal moots the court fight, while a failed repeal strengthens the state’s position and the national contagion argument. The ballot-language fight is already in court: on Aug. 7, 2026 a Thurston County judge upheld the government-drafted fiscal-impact disclosure that will appear beside the measure, and an emergency appeal reached the state Supreme Court on Aug. 10, racing the Aug. 21 county ballot-finalization deadline. No Supreme Court action had been reported as of Aug. 14. Separately, a Department of Revenue analysis in the I-645 fiscal-impact statement (Washington State Standard, Aug. 12, 2026) raised the first-year collection estimate to $3.1 billion from $2.7 billion and the household count to 25,000 from 21,000; the September official forecast is the first that may incorporate the higher figures.

events.title: The 62F tax-cap question (Question 5).
events.detail: Chapter 62F is the 1986 law that refunds taxpayers when state tax collections grow faster than wages; it triggered in 2022, returning about $3 billion. The ballot question rewrites the formula two ways: it rebases the cap to actual collections and pulls Fair Share surtax revenue into the capped base. Modeled effect (MTF): the cap would have triggered in four of the last ten years, with refunds of roughly $269 to $1,095 per filer. Potential impact: passage converts the surtax’s over-performance into automatic refund pressure, effectively a second round of the Fair Share fight; defeat leaves the surtax revenue fully outside the cap and removes the main structural check on its growth. A second front opened in late July: the state Senate voted 31–8 on July 23, 2026 to fold a 62F rewrite into the economic development bill, replacing the cap formula with a trigger at 7.5% of statewide personal income; the provision sits in a six-member House-Senate conference as of Aug. 14, and new legislative rules allow that conference to run as late as early January (MassINC, Aug. 14, 2026), so it may not resolve before Election Day; if enacted it would complicate or moot the ballot question.

events.title: Five of nine state Supreme Court seats on the ballot.
events.detail: A wave of retirements and appointments put a majority of the court’s seats up in one cycle. Whoever wins will almost certainly decide the Petter appeal in 2027, the final ruling on whether the millionaires tax survives. Potential impact: this is the rare election where judicial races directly determine a multi-billion-dollar tax outcome; both sides’ spending and candidate positioning on Culliton-era precedent are the tells to watch.

events.title: Legislative races.
events.detail: Vermont’s 2026 wealth-tax package (investment income taxes plus a new top-1% bracket, roughly $170M per year by 2028 per reported committee materials) died because Gov. Scott opposed it and Democrats lost their veto-proof supermajority in 2024. The package is pre-built and legislators expect the debate to resume in 2027. Potential impact: a restored two-thirds supermajority removes the only binding constraint; Vermont could then enact over a veto in the 2027 session, making these down-ballot races one of the highest-leverage tax events in the country.

events.title: Governorship and both chambers.
events.detail: Gov. Lamont has publicly opposed income tax rate increases and no high-income bill advanced in 2026, but the legislature’s progressive caucus has pushed surtax proposals repeatedly, and a statewide mansion tax proposal surfaced this year (Foley Wealth Tax Watch). Potential impact: Connecticut is a one-election state; a governor aligned with the caucus converts blocked proposals into live vehicles in 2027.

events.title: Constitutional amendment capping the income tax rate at 3.5%.
events.detail: North Carolina’s 2026 budget (S.L. 2026-41 / S.B. 257, Sec. 44.1, signed July 7, 2026) rewrote G.S. 105-153.7 to replace the trigger-dependent schedule with date-certain cuts: 3.99% for 2026, 3.49% for tax years 2027 to 2029, 3.24% for 2030 to 2032, and 2.99% after 2032, with revenue triggers permitting further quarter-point reductions to a 2.49% floor. The companion legislatively referred amendment, approved by both chambers in May 2026, would lower the constitutional income tax cap from 7% (approved by voters in 2018) to 3.5%; a second referred amendment on the same ballot would limit local property tax increases. Why it matters here: a 3.5% ceiling would make North Carolina the largest state with a hard constitutional bar against any future high-earner bracket, converting the cut-side divergence into constitutional text.

events.title: Four states vote on raising their own initiative thresholds; Missouri’s failed.
events.detail: Four states put measures before voters making their citizen-initiative processes harder to use (higher signature requirements or approval thresholds; Utah’s SJR 2 targets tax measures specifically). RESOLVED (MO): on Aug. 4, 2026, Missouri voters decisively rejected Amendment 4, which would have required citizen-initiated constitutional amendments to also carry a majority in every congressional district, 80.3% to 19.7%; all eight congressional districts voted no, and the companion Amendment 5, which would have created a path toward eliminating the individual income tax, also failed with 83.3% opposed (Missouri Independent, Aug. 4–5; Springfield Daily Citizen, Aug. 6, 2026). Utah, North Dakota, and South Dakota vote Nov. 3. Why it matters here: the initiative pathway is how wealth taxes reach voters where legislatures will not act, California’s Prop 40 route. Every state that raises its threshold closes that door a little, and Missouri’s emphatic rejection is the first 2026 data point that voters will defend the open door; the November results reshape the Ballot Access layer of the map and the long-run geography of where these fights can even occur.

events.title: Surtax phase one begins collecting: 1% on income over $1M.
events.detail: The first new-state surtax collection since Massachusetts. First-year revenue against the roughly $142M full-phase-in estimate becomes the next data point in the national argument, and the compliance experience (estimated payments, withholding on the new bracket) previews the 2% and 3% steps.

events.title: The 13% bracket on income over $1M (joint) takes effect (Act 24).
events.detail: Hawaii becomes the second-highest state rate after California’s 13.3%. Watch first-year filer behavior in a state with unusual migration friction (an island economy) and whether the dormant Rhoads wealth tax bill (1% on net assets over $20M) is refiled on the strength of the new bracket’s revenue.

events.title: Cut-side steps take effect: NE 3.99%, MT 5.4%, IN 2.9%, MS 3.75%.
events.detail: The other half of the national divergence: enacted, date-certain reductions in four states the same day two states raise. The widening spread between the two Americas is the backdrop for every migration and competitiveness argument in the raising states.

events.title: Does the Democratic trifecta refile the high-income bills.
events.detail: Virginia became a full Democratic trifecta in January 2026 when Gov. Spanberger took office. HB 979 (new 8% and 10% brackets at $600K and $1M) and HB 378 (a 3.8% net investment income tax) were filed in 2026 and died at the March adjournment; the governor neither endorsed nor pledged to sign them, and state revenues ran 2.9% ahead of forecast. Potential impact: refiling with leadership support in the roughly 46-day short session would make Virginia the first Southern state with a live millionaire-bracket vehicle; both chambers are on the Nov. 2027 ballot, which cuts both ways on appetite.

events.title: Does the wealth-tax package return, and with whose name on it.
events.detail: The tell is sponsorship: a rank-and-file refile repeats 2026, but House or Senate leadership sponsorship signals a decision to spend capital, especially if November restored a supermajority. The package’s contents (investment income taxes plus a top-1% bracket) are already drafted.

events.title: First high-income vehicle from the trifecta, or another quiet session.
events.detail: Minnesota already taxes net investment income over $1M at 1% (enacted 2023, effective tax year 2024) and has the political composition to go further, but no bill has been filed. A filed vehicle moves it up the risk board immediately; another quiet session confirms the 2023 measure as the ceiling for now.

events.title: Petter reaches the state Supreme Court.
events.detail: The final constitutional test of the millionaires tax, decided by the bench the November elections just shaped, and mooted if I-645 repealed the tax. The question is whether the court reaffirms Culliton (income is property, graduated rates unconstitutional) or extends the 2023 excise reasoning to an income tax. Potential impact: the ruling either voids the revised $3.1 billion first-year projection before first collections in 2029, or formally ends the constitutional barrier that has defined Washington tax policy since 1933, with immediate contagion effects on Oregon’s 2028 plans.

events.title: FY2027-28 budget: does the NYC income surtax return.
events.detail: Mamdani’s $5.5B package, including a 2% NYC surtax on high earners, was rejected in 2026; the pied-a-terre tax and state aid closed the gap instead. City budget documents project deficits in FY2028-29, and Gov. Hochul has publicly opposed income tax rate increases. Potential impact: the budget shows whether the pied-a-terre tax bought a durable truce or one year; a surtax revival against projected gaps would be the largest single high-earner tax fight in the country by dollar value.

events.title: Initiative filing deadline with the Attorney General (first Wednesday of August).
events.detail: The gateway for the 2028 ballot. Watch for: a refiled income tax cut, which Republican gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve has publicly vowed to lead for 2028 after the SJC removed the 2026 version (State House News, June 2026; under the Article 48 calendar no 2028 petition can be filed before this 2027 window, and none had been filed as of Aug. 14, 2026); and any statutory filing on capital gains rates or the estate tax, the two expansion routes that remain open without a constitutional amendment (the surtax itself cannot be expanded before a 2030 amendment ballot at the earliest). Potential impact: what gets filed here defines the entire 2028 Massachusetts fight.

events.title: FY2027 Fair Share certification.
events.detail: Year four of the revenue number driving national adoption: $2.2B, then $2.99B, then $3.38B, each more than double the original $1.2B estimate. The revenue is capital-gains-heavy and has only existed in a rising market. Potential impact: another beat extends the proponents’ best argument into the 2028 cycle; a first miss or decline is the first empirical crack, and every state watching will reprice.

events.title: Surtax phase two: 2%.
events.detail: The ratchet’s second step, arriving during the 2028 session in which the broader Fair Share package (including the 1% financial-assets tax) will be pressed again under the governor elected in November 2026.

events.title: The 9.9% tax takes effect, if it survived.
events.detail: Assuming the tax survived both the Supreme Court and the I-645 repeal vote, it attaches to income earned from this date, with first returns and payments in 2029. Withholding, estimated-payment behavior, and any pre-effective-date relocations become the first hard data on a new-state income tax at this rate.

events.title: Next constitutional-amendment election.
events.detail: Illinois’s flat-tax clause (Art. IX, Sec. 3) forecloses any graduated surtax by statute; HJRCA 21 (a 3% surtax over $1M) missed the 2026 ballot deadline. Nov. 2028 is the next opportunity, and the 2020 graduated-tax amendment’s 53-47 defeat is the base rate. Potential impact: passage would unlock the largest currently-barred state; a second defeat likely closes the question for a decade.

events.title: Next initiative election.
events.detail: IP 70 (a 2% annual wealth tax over $30M) failed to qualify in 2026, with press accounts of its filings reporting about $2,325 raised against a 117,173-signature requirement. Oregon’s open initiative process (simple majority) keeps the door structurally open; whether 2028 brings a funded campaign depends heavily on the CA Prop 40 result and the WA court outcome.

AK.name: Alaska
AK.ballotNote: Initiative for statutes only (10% of last vote, spread across three-quarters of house districts). Initiatives may not appropriate funds or dedicate revenue, which constrains tax-and-spend measures.
AK.currentNote: No state income tax. PFD dividend.
AK.futureNote: No personal income tax; the individual income tax was repealed in 1980. No high-income or wealth tax measure tracked.

HI.name: Hawaii
HI.ballotNote: No statewide citizen initiative or referendum process. Tax changes require legislative action; constitutional amendments reach voters only by legislative referral.
HI.slated: 13% bracket on income over $1M (joint) takes effect tax year 2027 (Act 24 / SB 3125).
HI.currentNote: 11% top rate for 2026 (brackets 1.4% to 11%). SB 3125 (Act 24, signed May 21, 2026) enacted a new 13% bracket on income over $1M joint ($500K single, $750K head of household), effective for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2026 (tax year 2027); DOTAX estimates about 2,300 returns. The separate proposed 1-point increase on the top three brackets was dropped; the 2024 middle-income cuts were preserved (joint filers up to $350K, single up to $175K).
HI.futureNote: The 13% bracket effective 2027 is enacted law (Act 24, SB 3125, signed May 21, 2026) and is recorded as a slated change, not risk; it would be the second-highest state rate after California's 13.3%. Remaining forward risk is the Rhoads wealth tax bill (1% on net assets over $20M), introduced in successive sessions without advancing. Composite 52.

proposals.title: 13% Millionaire Bracket, Enacted (effective 2027)
proposals.structure: New 13% bracket on income over $1M joint ($500K single), signed into law May 21, 2026, effective for tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2026. A separately proposed 1-point increase on the top three brackets was dropped in conference.
proposals.status: ENACTED (Act 24). Takes effect tax year 2027; 2026 top rate remains 11%.

proposals.title: 1% Wealth Tax on $20M+ Net Assets
proposals.structure: 1% annual tax on net assets above $20 million. Broadest definition of wealth among current state proposals.
proposals.status: Refiled across multiple sessions; has not advanced.

WA.name: Washington
WA.ballotNote: Initiative for statutes only (8% of last gubernatorial vote), direct or to the legislature; no citizen-initiated constitutional amendments. The legislature may amend an initiated statute by two-thirds vote within two years, simple majority after.
WA.slated: 9.9% tax on income over $1M takes effect Jan. 1, 2028, with first collections in 2029 (SB 6346); implementation is contingent on the pending Petter v. Dept. of Revenue litigation and on Initiative 645, the repeal measure certified for the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot on July 15, 2026.
WA.currentNote: SB 6346 signed March 30, 2026: 9.9% on income above $1M, effective Jan 1, 2028, first collections 2029. No general wage income tax until then, but WA already taxes capital gains: 7%, plus an additional 2.9% on gains over $1M for a 9.9% top tier (ESSB 5813, signed May 20, 2025, retroactive to Jan 1, 2025; WA DOR special notice). Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% income tax and bar income taxes generally, was certified for the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot on July 15, 2026.
WA.futureNote: The enacted 9.9% tax (effective Jan. 1, 2028) is recorded as a slated change contingent on litigation, not as risk. Petter v. Dept. of Revenue (filed April 9, 2026, Klickitat County; counsel includes former AG Rob McKenna and former Justice Phil Talmadge) challenges it on Culliton v. Chase (1933) uniformity grounds; no ruling reported as of August 14, 2026. In Heywood v. Hobbs (order filed May 4, 2026), the WA Supreme Court unanimously held ESSB 6346 falls within Art. II Sec. 1's support-of-state-government exception to the referendum power; constitutionality was expressly not addressed. Initiative 645 (Let's Go Washington), which would repeal SB 6346 and prohibit state and local taxes on individual income, was certified for the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot on July 15, 2026: more than 500,000 signatures were submitted by the July 2 deadline against a 308,911 requirement, and the Secretary of State validated the measure on a 3% sample. The I-645 ballot-language fight moved in August: on Aug. 7, 2026 a Thurston County judge upheld the public-investment-impact disclosure that will appear beside the measure, and an emergency appeal was filed with the state Supreme Court on Aug. 10, ahead of the Aug. 21 county ballot-finalization deadline. No Supreme Court action had been reported as of Aug. 14. A Department of Revenue analysis in the I-645 fiscal-impact statement (Washington State Standard, Aug. 12, 2026) raised first-year collections to $3.1 billion from $2.7 billion and the household count to 25,000 from 21,000; the September official forecast is the first that may incorporate the higher figures. Five of nine Supreme Court seats are on the Nov. 2026 ballot. Forward risk scored here covers expansion beyond the enacted law; no such vehicle is filed, and the certified repeal initiative cuts risk the other way. Composite 57.

OR.name: Oregon
OR.ballotNote: Direct initiative for statutes (6%) and amendments (8%), simple majority. IP 70 (wealth tax) attempted this path in 2026 but failed to qualify, missing the July 2 signature deadline.
OR.futureNote: IP 70 (2% annual wealth tax over $30M) failed to qualify, missing the July 2, 2026 signature deadline; press accounts of its campaign finance filings reported about $2,325 raised against a 117,173-signature requirement. The estate tax repeal initiative also failed to qualify. The next election at which an initiative can appear is Nov. 2028, outside this horizon; no 2027 legislative vehicle is filed. Composite 44, capped at Low.

proposals.title: 2% Annual Wealth Tax on $30M+
proposals.structure: 2% annual tax on net worth above $30M. Would affect ~4,600 Oregonians. Would be the first ongoing (not one-time) state wealth tax in US history.
proposals.status: FAILED TO QUALIFY. The measure missed the July 2, 2026 signature deadline and will not appear on the November ballot (Law360, July 6). The campaign needed 117,173 valid signatures; press accounts of its campaign finance filings reported only about $2,325 raised. The estate tax repeal initiative and the tax-cut measures also failed to qualify.

CA.name: California
CA.ballotNote: Direct initiative for statutes (5% of last gubernatorial vote) and constitutional amendments (8%), simple majority to pass, 180-day window. The most heavily used process in the country; the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act travels this path.
CA.currentNote: 1% MHST on $1M+ (approved 2004 as Prop 63, in effect since 2005) plus 12.3% top bracket = 13.3% top combined.
CA.futureNote: Four tax measures interact on the November ballot. Proposition 40 (one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax) faces two counter-measures: Proposition 41 (audit and spending-limit routing) and Proposition 42 (bars new taxes on ownership of personal property, applying to same-ballot measures); if conflicting measures pass together, only the highest vote total takes effect, so Prop 40 can win its own vote and still be nullified. Proposition 3 (a California Teachers Association-backed measure making permanent the Prop 30/Prop 55 rates on high incomes, otherwise scheduled to expire after tax year 2030) would prevent the 12.3%/13.3% top brackets from sunsetting; it reaches single filers from about $361,000. Building a Better California, the opposition committee co-founded by Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt, has reported more than $118 million raised, including $102 million contributed personally by Brin per filings disclosed through Aug. 7, 2026 (SF Standard; SF Examiner reports Yes on 40 at $31.4 million and combined Prop 40/41/42 committees at $140 million). The California Democratic Party endorsed Prop 40 in a narrow executive-board vote in early August 2026 (CalMatters). Composite 86.

proposals.title: 5% One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires
proposals.structure: One-time 5% tax on net worth above $1B, applying to individuals and applicable trusts resident on Jan. 1, 2026, structured as a combined initiated constitutional amendment and statute (AG title, no. 25-0024A1). Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally excluded; covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property. Due 2027, with a costlier five-year installment option. LAO: applies to roughly 200 billionaires; revenues in the tens of billions spread over several years, with a likely ongoing decrease in state income tax revenues of hundreds of millions per year. Allocation: 90% health care, 10% food assistance and education.
proposals.status: OFFICIALLY QUALIFIED June 17, 2026 (Secretary of State: 980,438 valid signatures vs. 874,641 required); designated Proposition 40 for the Nov. 3 ballot. SEIU-UHW offered to withdraw it if Newsom backed a 2% legislative version; he refused, and the June 25 withdrawal deadline passed. Newsom, Becerra, and Hilton all opposed; several progressive organizations and labor groups announced opposition in June 2026. Two counter-measures share the ballot: Proposition 41 (audits of programs funded by new special taxes; routes new special-tax revenue through the state spending limit) and Proposition 42 (AG no. 25-0041A1: bars new state taxes on the ownership or control of personal property, including financial assets, business interests, and intellectual property, and bars retroactive taxes; expressly applies to taxes on the same ballot). Under the conflicting-measures rule, if conflicting measures pass together, only the one with the highest vote total takes effect. Building a Better California, the opposition committee co-founded by Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt, has reported more than $118 million raised, including $102 million personally from Brin per filings disclosed through Aug. 7, 2026; supporters report $31.4 million (SF Examiner). Collectively the committees for and against Propositions 40, 41, and 42 have raised $140 million. The California Democratic Party endorsed the measure in a narrow executive-board vote in early August 2026, and the California Nurses Association has also endorsed; Newsom and Becerra remain opposed and SEIU California is neutral.

proposals.title: Top Income Tax Rate Permanence
proposals.structure: Makes California's top income tax brackets permanent, removing the sunset on the high-earner rates first approved in 2012 (Prop 30) and extended by Prop 55 (2016) through tax year 2030. Reaches income above roughly $361K single / $721K joint (indexed). Revenue to public education.
proposals.status: Certified as Proposition 3 for the November 3, 2026 ballot, one of 14 statewide measures, sharing the ballot with Propositions 40, 41, and 42.

NV.name: Nevada
NV.ballotNote: Statutes go to the legislature first (indirect); constitutional amendments must pass at two consecutive general elections, a built-in two-year delay and double campaign cost.
NV.currentNote: No state income tax. Sales-tax dependent.
NV.futureNote: The Nevada Constitution prohibits a tax on the personal income of natural persons (Art. 10, Sec. 1(9)). No repeal measure tracked.

ID.name: Idaho
ID.ballotNote: Initiative for statutes only, 6% statewide plus 6% in 18 of 35 legislative districts, one of the toughest distribution requirements.
ID.futureNote: Republican trifecta. Top rate 5.3% for 2026 (Tax Foundation). No high-income or wealth tax proposal tracked.

UT.name: Utah
UT.ballotNote: Initiative for statutes only (direct and indirect paths). SJR 2, on the November 2026 ballot, would require 60% approval for any initiative that raises taxes, and 2025 laws added funding-disclosure and publication-cost burdens.
UT.futureNote: Republican trifecta. Rate 4.5% for 2026 (Tax Foundation). No increase proposal tracked. SJR 2, raising the initiative threshold for tax measures, is on the Nov. 2026 ballot.

AZ.name: Arizona
AZ.ballotNote: Direct initiative for statutes (10%) and amendments (15%), but Prop 132 (2022) requires 60% approval for any measure that enacts a tax.
AZ.futureNote: Flat 2.5% rate in effect since 2023. Divided government (Democratic governor, Republican legislature). No increase proposal tracked.

MT.name: Montana
MT.ballotNote: Direct initiative for statutes (5%) and amendments (10% with district distribution), majority to pass.
MT.slated: Top rate falls to 5.4% in 2027 under enacted law.
MT.currentNote: 5.65% top rate as of Jan 1, 2026 (HB 337), cut from 5.9%.
MT.futureNote: Top rate 5.65% for 2026, with a scheduled reduction to 5.4% in 2027. Republican trifecta. No increase proposal tracked.

WY.name: Wyoming
WY.ballotNote: Initiative for statutes only (15% of last vote with distribution across two-thirds of counties), among the hardest processes in the country and rarely used.
WY.futureNote: No personal income tax; none has been enacted in state history. No proposal tracked.

CO.name: Colorado
CO.ballotNote: Direct initiative for statutes and amendments (5% of Secretary of State vote). Amendments need 55% approval plus signatures from each senate district (Amendment 71). TABOR cuts both ways: every tax increase, however proposed, requires voter approval. Initiative 195, a graduated-rate income tax measure, submitted signatures Aug. 3, 2026, now pending verification; it competes with Initiative 232, which would cap the rate at 4.4%.

MA.name: Massachusetts
MA.ballotNote: Indirect process only, under Article 48. Initiative amendments need signatures (3% of the gubernatorial vote, 74,574 this cycle) plus approval of 25% of legislators (50 of 200) in two successive joint sessions, a minimum four-year runway. Citizen petitions also face subject-matter limits: the original citizen Fair Share amendment was struck from the 2018 ballot by the SJC (Anderson v. Attorney General, 2018) for combining the tax with spending earmarks. The version enacted in 2022 was a legislatively referred amendment, which needs a majority of two joint sessions and is exempt from those exclusions. A statutory wealth tax would conflict with the proportionality requirement as construed by the SJC, and the constitution's uniformity and proportionality requirements, leaving the amendment path as the remaining route. SJC gatekeeping cuts both ways: in June 2026 the court removed the 5%-to-4% income tax CUT initiative from the ballot in Finfer v. Attorney General (SJC-13885, June 18, 2026) over a significantly misleading AG summary of the capital-gains effect. The statute track is in active use this cycle: the Chapter 62F tax-cap question was certified for the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot as Question 5 (State Revenue Limit and Rebate), one of nine statewide questions, tying the modern record set in 1972, 1976, and 1994, with numbers assigned by the Elections Division of the Secretary of the Commonwealth.
MA.currentNote: 4% Fair Share surtax on income over $1,107,750 (2026 threshold, indexed; Mass.gov). Top combined 9%. DOR reported final FY2026 collections of $3.38B (July 2026), up 13% year over year and more than twice the original $1.2B estimate for the third straight year, against the $2.4B the budget planned to use (actuals certify Oct. 2026). Prior years: ~$2.2B FY2024, ~$2.99B FY2025.
MA.futureNote: Press reports state that union leaders are exploring a CA-style billionaire wealth tax for the Commonwealth; no petition has been filed as of August 14, 2026. The countervailing measure, a ballot initiative cutting the 5% base rate to 4%, was REMOVED from the November ballot by the SJC on June 18, 2026 (the AG's summary was ruled significantly misleading for omitting the capital gains cut). Republican gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve has publicly vowed to lead a 2028 refiling of the cut (State House News, June 2026); under the Article 48 calendar no 2028 petition can be filed before the August 2027 window, and none has been filed as of Aug. 14, 2026. Structural note: expanding the surtax itself requires a constitutional amendment, since Article 121 authorizes exactly 4% above the indexed threshold, and the earliest amendment ballot is 2030, outside this window. Statutory routes do remain open inside it: Article 44 permits different rates on different classes of income, so a long-term capital gains increase is available by ordinary legislation, as is estate tax expansion (an excise). No such bill is filed. The model computes Massachusetts at 68 points, the second-highest composite after California: budget pressure scores 12 of 15 on the documented growth in structural one-time reliance from roughly $1.1B to $1.9B across the FY2025-FY2027 budgets (MTF analysis), and contagion scores the maximum 10 on two adjacent 2026 enactments (Rhode Island and Maine) that cited the Fair Share results, plus the Vermont package modeled on it. The published tier is the computed tier. The same coalition's Chapter 62F tax-cap question was certified for the November ballot in July 2026 (second-round signatures submitted by the early-July deadline): it would rebase the cap to actual prior-year collections and bring Fair Share surtax revenue inside the calculation, making refunds far more frequent. MTF modeling finds the revised cap would have triggered in four of the last ten years, with equal refunds of $269 to $1,095 per filer. Because it pulls surtax revenue into the cap, its outcome directly shapes the Fair Share expansion fight. A second 62F front opened in late July: the Senate voted 31-8 on July 23, 2026 to fold a rewrite into the economic development bill, replacing the cap formula with a trigger at 7.5% of statewide personal income; the provision sits in a six-member House-Senate conference as of Aug. 14, 2026, and new legislative rules allow that conference to run as late as early January (MassINC, Aug. 14, 2026), so it may not resolve before Election Day; if enacted it would complicate or moot the ballot question (CommonWealth Beacon).

SC.name: South Carolina
SC.ballotNote: No statewide citizen initiative or referendum process. Tax changes require legislative action; constitutional amendments reach voters only by legislative referral.
SC.currentNote: 5.21% top rate for tax year 2026. H.4216 (Act 110, signed March 30, 2026) restructured the income tax to a two-bracket system (1.99% up to $30,000; 5.21% above), superseding the prior three-bracket structure, whose top rate was 6.0% for tax year 2025 under a temporary reduction from the statutory 6.2%.
SC.futureNote: H.4216 (2026) restructured to a 5.21% top rate and provides revenue-triggered reductions that continue until the top rate reaches 1.99% and then phase the tax toward elimination (SCDOR). No increase proposal tracked.

DC.name: District of Columbia
DC.ballotNote: Initiative process exists but measures may not appropriate funds, which effectively bars tax-and-spend initiatives. Tax changes run through the Council.
DC.currentNote: 10.75% bracket on income over $1M (enacted 2021, effective tax year 2022), among the highest millionaire brackets in the country.
DC.futureNote: One of five jurisdictions to raise top rates since 2021 (Tax Foundation); the 10.75% bracket was enacted in 2021, effective tax year 2022, and is current policy. No new high-income vehicle is pending before the Council. Council-only legislative pathway; no initiative process for tax measures. Composite 57.

GA.name: Georgia
GA.ballotNote: No statewide citizen initiative or referendum process. Tax changes require legislative action; constitutional amendments reach voters only by legislative referral.
GA.currentNote: 4.99% flat rate. HB 463 (signed May 11, 2026) accelerated the cut from 5.19% to 4.99% retroactive to Jan 1, 2026, reaching sub-5% three years ahead of schedule.
GA.futureNote: Long-term plan lowers the rate toward 3.99% via 0.125-point annual reductions if revenue targets are met. Republican trifecta.

FL.name: Florida
FL.ballotNote: Citizen initiative for constitutional amendments only, with a 60% approval requirement, and new taxes or fees imposed by amendment require two-thirds approval. HB 1205 (2025) added severe process restrictions including a $1M bond. One of the most tax-protective initiative regimes anywhere.
FL.currentNote: No state income tax. Constitutional barrier (Art. VII, Sec. 5).
FL.futureNote: The Florida Constitution prohibits a personal income tax (Art. VII); enacting one would require an amendment approved by 60% of voters, and Amendment 5 (2018) requires a two-thirds legislative vote for any new state tax. No proposal tracked.
